evidence.claim: At Los Olivos, passengers could continue by stagecoach over the pass from the narrow-gauge railway’s southern terminus.
evidence.quote: The southern terminus of the railroad was in front of Mattei's Tavern, where a stagecoach line continued over San Marcos Pass into Santa Barbara.

evidence.claim: At Los Olivos, passengers could continue by stagecoach over the pass from the narrow-gauge railway’s southern terminus.
evidence.quote: Los Olivos was connected by the narrow gauge railroad to points north as far as San Luis Obispo until the train made its last run in 1934.

evidence.claim: The mountain highway entered the state system in 1931 and received the number 154 in the 1964 renumbering.
evidence.quote: The highway from Santa Barbara through San Marcos Pass to what was Route 2 was added to the state highway system in 1931. The route renumbered to SR 154 by the 1964 state highway renumbering.

evidence.claim: Cachuma is a reservoir beside Route 154, formed when the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation built Bradbury Dam across the Santa Ynez River in 1953.
evidence.quote: Cachuma Lake is a reservoir in the Santa Ynez Valley of central Santa Barbara County, California on the Santa Ynez River adjoining the north side of California State Route 154. The artificial lake was created by the construction of Bradbury Dam, a 201 ft (61 m) earth-fill structure built by the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation in 1953.

evidence.claim: The project stored water for regional cities and irrigation.
evidence.quote: intended to provide long-term water storage and delivery to Santa Barbara and other cities throughout the region as well as provide water for irrigation.

evidence.claim: Its shoreline changes with the water supply: the reservoir spills in some years and drops below 10 percent of capacity in dry years.
evidence.quote: The water levels of the lake are highly variable, spilling in some years and receding to less than 10% of capacity in dry years.

evidence.claim: In October 2016, storage fell to approximately 7.3 percent of capacity. By January 15, 2023, successive storms had brought it nearly to capacity.
evidence.quote: approximately 7.3% of capacity.

evidence.claim: In October 2016, storage fell to approximately 7.3 percent of capacity.
evidence.quote: In October 2016, the lake approached low levels not seen since the construction of Bradbury Dam.

evidence.claim: By January 15, 2023, successive storms had brought it nearly to capacity.
evidence.quote: Several consecutive atmospheric river storms coming in from the Pacific in late-December, 2022 and early-January, 2023 dramatically raised the water level in the lake, from an average of 33% full in late December, to nearly 100% full by January 15, 2023

evidence.claim: Originally called Cachuma Dam, the structure was renamed in 1971 for local water-supply advocate C. W. Bradbury.
evidence.quote: Originally named the Cachuma Dam upon completion in 1953, the name was changed in 1971 to honor C. W. "Brad" Bradbury, a local water supply proponent.
